tiers.name: Market leaders
tiers.note: Category-defining companies. Their moves set the reference price for everyone else.

tiers.name: Smaller companies
tiers.note: Less reach, but often early signs of a trend.

patterns.name: Price increase
patterns.definition: List price goes up, with no bigger structural change.

patterns.name: Price cut
patterns.definition: List price goes down, for everyone or for new buyers only.

patterns.name: Bundling
patterns.definition: Products or features folded into one plan or subscription.

patterns.name: Unbundling
patterns.definition: One product split into parts sold separately, or an included feature becomes a paid add-on.

patterns.name: Tier consolidation
patterns.definition: Plans removed or merged: fewer ways to buy.

patterns.name: New tier
patterns.definition: A new plan added between or below existing ones.

patterns.name: Rename & reposition
patterns.definition: Plans or features renamed or reworded, with no price or limit change.

patterns.name: Limits tighten
patterns.definition: Less included for the same price: usage, seats, caps.

patterns.name: Limits loosen
patterns.definition: More included for the same price.

patterns.name: Minimums
patterns.definition: Minimum seats, spend or purchase added, raised, lowered or removed.

patterns.name: Billing terms
patterns.definition: When or how you pay changes: upfront, monthly-only, annual-only.

patterns.name: New billing units
patterns.definition: The unit you’re charged by changes: credits, compute units, per-user vs bundles.

patterns.name: AI gets a meter
patterns.definition: AI usage becomes metered: credits, allowances, top-ups.

patterns.name: AI moves between tiers
patterns.definition: AI features move to a cheaper tier, a pricier tier or a paid add-on.

patterns.name: AI costs pass through
patterns.definition: Model or inference price changes passed on to customers.

patterns.name: Free plans as funnels
patterns.definition: A free or entry plan is added, expanded or tightened to drive upgrades.

changes.short: Pro’s “Premium tools” relabelled “AI tools”, with a new fair-use footnote.
changes.headline: Canva relabelled the tools in its Pro plan as AI tools and added a fair-use note, the first stated limit on them.
rows: AI tools (resize, translate, remove background, and more)
changes.who: Pro subscribers who use these tools heavily.
changes.read: Calling them AI tools and adding fair use prepares the ground for metering later. For now nothing costs more.
changes.caveat: We didn’t search for an announcement: wording changes rarely have one.

changes.short: Free Starter plan removed; Core ($18–20 a month) is now the entry tier.
changes.headline: Replit removed its free Starter plan from the pricing page, so the cheapest way in is now the paid Core plan.
rows: Free agent usage on Core and Pro
changes.who: New users who would have started free.
changes.read: A free tier dropped once the paid product sells itself. Free usage now lives inside paid plans rather than as its own tier.
changes.caveat: The source shows the plan left the pricing page; it may still exist for existing users.

changes.short: Virtual Mail plans up $10–40 a month: Personal $29 → $39, Family $39 → $59, Family & Business $79 → $119.
changes.headline: LegalZoom raised all three Virtual Mail plans by a third to a half.
changes.who: Virtual Mail subscribers and new buyers.
changes.read: A steep increase on a side product few customers compare. Well above the typical increase we track (median +20%).

changes.short: Essentials now includes a channel manager (powered by SiteMinder) for Booking.com, Expedia and Airbnb.
changes.headline: Mews added a channel manager, powered by SiteMinder, to its entry Essentials plan.
changes.who: Small hotels on Essentials, who may no longer need a separate channel manager.
changes.read: Folding a partner product into the entry plan adds value without a price change and makes switching harder.

changes.short: GPU quota per notebook, training task or node doubled from 4 to 8.
changes.headline: OVHcloud doubled the GPU quota per task across its AI Notebooks, AI Training and AI Deploy products.
rows: GPUs per notebook, task or node
changes.who: Teams running larger AI workloads on OVHcloud.
changes.read: More headroom for big jobs at the same unit price, aimed at buyers comparing GPU access with the hyperscalers.

Coding agent and Slack agent add-ons merged into one, still $0.40 per agent minute.
Agent credit costs now disclosed: 25 credits per Assistant answer, 250 per automation update.
$19 Code Review plan removed; the cheapest plan is now Platform at $29 per user.
$2,000 flat license replaced by per-seat Essential ($2,000) and Core ($3,000, with AI tools).
New Basic plan at $23 per builder a month between Free and Pro, built around AI credits.
Team plan moves from per-seat pricing to a flat rate that includes 3 users.
Essential $17 → $19, Premium $27 → $29 a month.
New permanent free tier: 500 email verifications a month.
Voice cloning split out and limited to Enterprise and Agency plans, at 20,000 credits per clone.
WhatsApp marketing conversation rate up from €0.057 to €0.0658.
AI Search Analytics $158 → $82 a month, with tracked prompts halved from 100 to 50.
Enterprise now tracks up to 13 AI models, up from 12.
Surveys moved from the entry Comply plan up to Perform.
Usage-only pricing split into Self-serve, AI Data Team ($10,000 a month), Enterprise and a $9,000 pilot.
Automated data refresh and dashboards no longer listed on any plan.
Log ingestion on Professional goes from free to €0.50 per GB.
Premium plan now includes ecommerce, which was previously on higher plans only.
Essentials texts 100 → 250, email blasts 500 → 1,000, storage 25 → 50 GB a month.
Pro’s included AI usage up from $80 to $100 a month at the same $100 per user.
Daily project update emails now included on Starter.
Deposit and payment processing surcharge raised from 1% to 1.2%.
Web and mobile apps go from included to an extra from $3,500.
AI Charting Assistant: 600 free minutes plus overage replaced by flat tiers at $10, $20 and $40 a month.
Agent Hub moves down to Starter; Professional gets new agents but loses omni-channel automation.
changes.headline: HubSpot moved its Agent Hub (AI agents and Agent Builder) down to the Starter tier and reshuffled what Professional and Enterprise include.
rows: Removed; Content Agent and Nurture Agent (beta) added
changes.who: New and existing Starter customers gain agents; Professional customers lose a listed automation feature.
changes.read: Agents are metered by HubSpot Credits, so putting them on the cheapest tier widens the base that can spend credits. The plan price matters less than the usage it unlocks.
changes.caveat: Seen on several HubSpot pricing pages tracked separately by PricingSaaS; merged here into one change.

changes.short: Free plan gets Projects (up to 5); Max 5x and 20x lose annual billing.
changes.headline: Claude’s Free plan gained Projects, and the Max 5x and 20x plans can now only be paid monthly.
changes.who: Free users gain a feature. New Max buyers lose the annual option.
changes.read: Dropping annual billing on the top plans keeps prices flexible while usage costs are still moving. Giving Free users Projects is a funnel move toward Pro.

changes.short: Estimated voice-agent rate up from $0.056 to $0.06 a minute; speech-to-text add-ons cut.
changes.headline: Telnyx’s estimated cost for a production voice agent rose about 7% as one model’s rate went up 50%, while third-party speech-to-text got cheaper.
changes.who: Teams running voice agents on Telnyx.
changes.read: A model-cost increase passed straight through, softened by a cut elsewhere in the stack. Usage-priced AI products will keep moving like this as model prices shift.

changes.short: Starter ($99) and Growth ($399) removed; only a free trial and Enterprise remain.
changes.headline: Profound dropped its paid self-serve plans. Buyers now start on a free trial and move to a custom Enterprise contract.
changes.who: Small teams who would have bought Starter or Growth.
changes.read: A move up-market: fewer small accounts, more sales-led contracts. Small buyers lose a way in.

changes.short: Included concurrent calls cut from 10 to 4; getting 10 back needs the $29 Core plan.
changes.headline: Vapi cut the concurrent calls included at entry level from 10 to 4. Ten concurrent calls now require the paid Core plan.
changes.who: Developers on Vapi’s entry level.
changes.read: A limit cut that turns a free capability into a paid upgrade.

changes.short: Qwen3.7-Max inference up 25%: $2.00 → $2.50 input, $6.00 → $7.50 output per million tokens.
changes.headline: Together AI raised the price of Qwen3.7-Max serverless inference by 25%.
changes.who: Developers calling Qwen3.7-Max on Together.
changes.read: Inference prices don’t only fall. For popular open models, hosts are pricing to demand.

changes.short: Free plan on Android goes from unlimited words to 1,000 a week.
changes.headline: Wispr Flow capped its free plan on Android at 1,000 words a week, matching iPhone.
changes.who: Free Android users.
changes.read: Closing an unlimited loophole on one platform. A typical free-tier tightening once a product has traction.

changes.short: MiniMax H3 Max video quotas cut 4x on every tier (Max: 864 → 216 videos).
changes.headline: Krea cut monthly video-generation quotas for two MiniMax models by four times on all tiers.
rows: MiniMax H3 Max Turbo, Max tier
changes.who: Krea subscribers generating video.
changes.read: Expensive video models get rationed as their cost becomes clear.

changes.short: Explorer $144 → $149, Growth $375 → $379, Advanced $999 → $1,049 a month.
changes.headline: Lokalise raised all three self-serve plans by small amounts.
changes.who: New and renewing Lokalise customers.
changes.read: A routine list-price step.

changes.short: Essentials renamed Starter and nearly tripled in price, with more words and credits.
changes.headline: Koala’s entry plan went from $9 to $25 a month, with three times the word allowance and new AI features.
changes.who: New buyers of the entry plan.
changes.read: A cheap entry tier rebuilt around AI usage at a higher price.

changes.short: Standard £21 → £27, Plus £33 → £39 a month.
changes.headline: Soldo raised its two main plans by £6 a month each.
changes.who: Soldo customers on Standard and Plus.
changes.read: A flat increase with no packaging change.

changes.short: Starter adds a 4th concurrent build, unlimited team members, a 3rd private app and up to 40 free AI credits.
Premium ($125 a month) discontinued; its integrations, branding and AI auto-tagging move into Pro.
Starter loses AI-driven functional testing (now Professional and up) but gains a Visual AI MCP server.
Growth renders 10 → 200 and placement tests 10 → 100 a month; Free cut from 3 to 1 of each.
New AI credit allowances: 10,000, 20,000 and 40,000 a month by plan.
Free plan: unlimited contacts, but the 4,000 monthly emails only go to the 1,000 newest.
Basic AI tool limits cut on Pro (750 → 150) and Elite (1,000 → 750); Starter storage doubled.
Perplexity tracking moves to Enterprise only; Naver AI added on all plans.
Daily posting limits now apply per workspace instead of per user.
New entry Core plan at $179 a month (annual) for stores above 6,000 monthly orders.
LLM Gateway base fee cut from $400 to $200 a month plus usage; startup credits trimmed.
Role-based access control, previously Enterprise only, now included on every plan.
Standalone iOS Management plan removed.
Premium’s unlimited searches become pay-per-use after 30 free per category; Free gets case quotas.
Workers’ comp and auto claims move from included on Growth and Premium to per-claim billing.
New industry plans: Customer Service Cloud $224, Financial Services and Public Sector $149 per user a month.
New free GO plan; $199 PRO removed and PRO+ renamed PRO with custom pricing.
Annual quote ($5,400 a seat, $27K minimum) replaced by $450 a seat a month with mandatory annual prepay.
Pro plan ($1,440 a month) now annual-only; monthly billing removed.
Seedance 2.0 video credit costs cut about in half (720p 107 → 51 credits a second).
Free tier moves from 5 million metered tokens a month to unmetered fair use with daily rate limits.
GPT Image 2 replaced by two 2.5 variants; the lowest price per request falls from $0.225 to $0.035.
Starter renamed Essential, with a minimum of 5 teams now disclosed.
Timesheets per-user prices up about 10–15% (average $5.21 → $5.99 a user).
Migration services move from Scale to Growth, and Scale drops multi-feature spaces.
Payroll add-on base fee up from $39 to $49 a month.
SSO and SAML move from Growth to Enterprise only.
Volunteer and Prospect AI now included in the Giving Platform bundle, whose $242 starting price is now hidden.
Professional plan inbound routers cut from unlimited to 3 per team.
Annual billing with 20% off added; per-license prices fall (Medium $30 → $24); $238 add-ons discontinued.
Opus 5.5 replaces Opus 5 as the flagship at $4/$20 per million tokens, down from $5/$25.
changes.headline: Anthropic’s new flagship, Opus 5.5, costs 20% less than the Opus 5 model it replaces.
changes.who: API customers moving to the new flagship.
changes.read: Each new frontier model has launched cheaper than the last. The cut also lands the same day as OpenAI’s GPT-6 Sol and Luna release.

changes.short: “AI in Dropbox” goes live on Standard and Advanced, metered by AI credits.
changes.headline: Dropbox turned its “coming soon” AI teaser into a live feature on Standard and Advanced, with a monthly allowance of AI credits.
changes.who: Dropbox Standard and Advanced teams.
changes.read: A seat product adds a metered AI allowance instead of raising the seat price. The allowance size is the lever to watch.

changes.short: New cap of 50 automations per base on every plan.
changes.headline: Airtable added a limit of 50 automations per base to all plans, from Free to Enterprise Scale.
rows: Not limited on the pricing page
changes.who: Heavy automation users, especially on large bases.
changes.read: A new limit where none was shown. Small for most users; it matters for teams that run a lot of logic in one base.
changes.caveat: Reversed two days later: PricingSaaS’s week-41 review reports the cap was lifted to 75–200 per base, depending on the plan.

changes.short: Experiment results kept 3 months instead of 15 days for customers with a commitment.
changes.headline: Datadog extended experiment result retention from 15 days to 3 months for customers on an annual or month-to-month commitment.
changes.who: Product teams running experiments in Datadog under a commitment.
changes.read: Longer retention is offered as a reward for committing, which nudges pay-as-you-go customers toward contracts.

changes.short: Team plan goes from unlimited members to up to 200 users.
changes.headline: Cognition capped its Team plan at 200 users. It was previously sold with unlimited members and flex seats.
changes.who: Larger teams on the Team plan, who now need Enterprise.
changes.read: A classic ceiling that pushes big accounts into sales-led Enterprise deals.

changes.short: New Free plan: 1 project, 10 reports a day, no card required; AI Visibility excluded.
changes.headline: Semrush added a free plan for the first time, without its AI visibility features.
changes.who: New users trying Semrush.
changes.read: A free tier as a funnel, with the AI features kept behind the paywall as the upgrade reason.

changes.short: Log ingestion now metered: 20 GB included on Pro and Team, then $0.50 per GB.
changes.headline: Supabase started charging for log ingestion above an included amount.
changes.who: Projects with heavy logging.
changes.read: A new meter on something that used to be free. Small per unit, but it adds to the bill of busy projects.

changes.short: Basic plan’s AI video assets cut from 25 to 3 a month.
changes.headline: Synthesia cut the AI video assets included in its Basic plan from 25 to 3 a month.
changes.who: Basic plan users.
changes.read: The entry plan gets thinner so the next tier looks better.

changes.short: New Lite tier between Free and c.ai+, with partial access to premium chat styles.
changes.headline: Character.AI added a cheaper Lite tier between its free plan and c.ai+.
changes.who: Free users who wouldn’t pay for c.ai+.
changes.read: A middle step to convert free users who balk at the full price.

changes.short: AI credit allowances (1,000–6,000 a month) and form-submission caps added per plan.
changes.headline: A Zoho app’s restructured plans now include AI credit allowances of 1,000 to 6,000 a month, plus form-submission caps of 50 to 10,000 a month.
changes.who: Customers of the restructured app, on every plan.
changes.read: Zoho sells to price-sensitive small businesses, so its move to metered AI with included allowances suggests credits are becoming the default even at the low end.
changes.caveat: The feed doesn’t name which Zoho app changed.

changes.short: New standalone AI Voice Agents plan with a $100 monthly minimum; Custom renamed Enterprise.
changes.headline: Aircall added a standalone AI Voice Agents plan with a $100 monthly minimum and renamed its Custom plan to Enterprise.
changes.who: Businesses that want AI phone agents without buying more seats.
changes.read: Selling agents as their own plan, with a spend minimum instead of seats, lets Aircall charge for agents that do work humans on seats used to do. Expect more seat-based phone tools to split AI out this way.

changes.short: Professional $79 → $99, Advanced $149 → $199, Scale $349 → $449 a month.
changes.headline: Vista Social raised its three paid plans by 25–34%.
changes.who: New and renewing customers.
changes.read: A large step for a small tool; worth watching for churn signals.

changes.short: AI Review and AI Insights move from included to a paid add-on.
changes.headline: Oneflow moved AI contract review and insights out of its plans into a paid add-on.
rows: Paid add-on on Business and Enterprise
changes.who: Enterprise customers who used the AI features.
changes.read: Free AI during launch, paid once it proves useful.

changes.short: Usage-based AI credit billing pushed back from September to November 2026.
changes.headline: Teamwork.com delayed the start of AI credit billing by two months.
changes.who: Paid customers using AI features.
changes.read: A delay often means customers pushed back, or the meter wasn’t ready.

changes.short: Smallest credit pack ($25 for 1,500) removed; the minimum is now $50.
changes.headline: Pika removed its smallest credit top-up, doubling the minimum purchase.
changes.who: Light users who top up occasionally.
changes.read: Raising the minimum spend without touching the per-credit price.

changes.short: Mid-tier loses two-way Jira/Asana/ClickUp/Monday sync, client collaboration and AI features, moved to a new top Premium tier.
Hosting subrequest limit raised from 1,000 to 10,000 per request on paid plans.
App limits raised: Free and Basic 2 → 10 apps, Pro up to 10.
Storage raised: Pro 100 → 200 GB, Business 500 → 800 GB; Free now shows 5 GB.
Paid plans add free guest seats: 20 on Max, 10 on Plus.
New free-forever plan: one RCS agent in test mode with full builder access.
Prepaid credit bundles replaced by annual recruiting-volume commitments.
Pricing rebuilt around a prepaid balance with unit rates (email $15 a month, SMS $0.0035 a segment); new $24.95 dedicated IP add-on.
Kurrent AI features, previously Team and Enterprise only, now included on Free; Team gets agents instead.
Fine-tuning prices reset: GPT-OSS 20B $0.40 → $2.50, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning $0.80 → $0.40, Qwen3.8 27B $4.00 → $2.50 per million tokens.
Plus plan invited users go from 1 to unlimited.
Pricing now set by cloud accounts ($495 a month for 5), with a new 15-day free trial tier.
Free plan can no longer buy labels over the monthly limit (was €0.50 a label).
New Corporate Suite tier added, with AI fact-finding listed as an add-on.
Image editor removed from the Intelligence+ AI add-on (€19–29 a month).
Offerings cut from 8 to 4, and the $3,500 flat price replaced by custom pricing.
Monthly credits raised on every plan (Basic 1,500 → 2,000, Professional 14,400 → 18,000).
Every Gloo Code plan now includes every agent and model, replacing tier-gated model access.
Agent-task and credit limits replaced by goal and agent concurrency limits.
Legal Capture and Legal Visor lose unlimited hours and mobile app access.
Pay-per-agent-run pricing replaced by agent-month subscriptions, led by a $250K-a-year governance layer.
New Scale plan at $419 a month between Business and Circle Plus.
Agent add-on moves from a $1,000 one-time setup to $10 per user a month (3-user minimum).
Koala AI MCP integration out of beta and included on every paid plan (was Professional and up).
AI agent features, once exclusive to the $190 Business+ tier, now start at the $50 Individual tier.
Dialer no longer included on Free; now promoted as a Pro feature.
Offline demos and deal intelligence move from Premium to Growth; Media to Demo moves to Free.
Premium bundles two new apps (Vision, Rhythm) at the same $49 a month.
Free verification add-on broadened from catch-all addresses to all emails.
Agentforce 1 Editions renamed Agentforce Max; included Flex Credits up from 2.5M to 2.75M a year.

changes.who: Customers on Salesforce’s top editions.
changes.read: More included credits at the same price encourages more agent usage, which is where Salesforce wants revenue to grow.

changes.short: Assistant credits cut 30% (Starter 2,300 → 1,600; Pro 13,700 → 9,600); top-ups now for sale.
changes.headline: n8n cut the monthly credits for its AI building assistant by 30% and, for the first time, lets customers buy more.
changes.who: n8n Cloud customers using the Assistant.
changes.stated: n8n says it moved everyone to a newer model, so the Assistant needs fewer credits for the same work.
changes.read: The fourth change to this allowance since July. Cutting the included amount while opening top-ups turns a fixed perk into a meter.

changes.short: Plans renamed Free/Lite/Pro; Lite $43 → $49 with fewer seats; Pro seats capped at 10.
changes.headline: beehiiv renamed its plans, raised the middle one and cut seats on both paid plans, while raising Pro’s subscriber cap.
changes.who: Paid newsletter creators, especially teams.
changes.read: Seats get tighter while audience limits loosen: beehiiv prices the team, not the list.

changes.short: LangChain Compute Units ($1.50) retired; all usage now in Standard Units ($1.00), rates rescaled.
changes.headline: LangChain replaced its compute unit with a cheaper-looking standard unit and rescaled every rate.
changes.who: LangSmith customers on usage billing.
changes.read: A unit change is hard to compare. The allowances went up by about the price ratio, so the net effect is roughly neutral.

changes.short: Plus plan seats raised from 40 to 50; AI Actions quotas removed from the plan cards.
changes.headline: PagerDuty raised the Plus plan’s seat limit and stopped listing AI Actions quotas on its plans.
changes.who: Plus customers near the seat cap; AI Actions users.
changes.read: Hiding a quota usually means it’s being reworked, not removed. Watch for a new AI price.
changes.caveat: Removing the quota from the page doesn’t tell us whether AI Actions became unlimited.

changes.short: Konnect split into AI, API and Event Management, each sold separately from $25 a month plus usage.
changes.headline: Kong split its Konnect platform into three products you can buy separately, each with Plus and Enterprise tiers.
rows: AI, API or Event Management, separately
changes.who: New Konnect buyers.
changes.read: Unbundling lets Kong sell AI gateway use on its own, without the full API platform.

changes.short: Advanced plan ($49 a month) removed as the page drops its workflow-automation tiers.
changes.headline: Pipedream removed its $49 Advanced plan along with its workflow-automation tiers.
changes.who: Prospective buyers of workflow automation.
changes.read: A product refocus showing up as a pricing change.

changes.short: Workflows max compute cut from 8 CPU/32 GB to 4 CPU/16 GB; Key Value RAM raised.
changes.headline: Render halved the largest compute option for Workflows and raised the memory ceiling for Key Value.
changes.who: Workflows users needing large instances.
changes.read: Removing the biggest option caps how much a single workflow can use.

changes.short: Free plan no longer lists selling products, courses and brand offers.
changes.headline: Linktree’s free plan no longer shows selling products, courses or brand offers as included.
changes.who: Free creators who sell through Linktree.
changes.read: Monetization features move behind the paywall.
changes.caveat: Based on what the free plan card lists; Linktree may not have removed the feature itself.

changes.short: Data Center edition removed; its autoscaling and high-performance features now listed on Enterprise.
changes.headline: SonarSource removed the Data Center edition from its server lineup; its autoscaling and high-performance features are now listed on Enterprise.
changes.who: Large self-hosted customers who bought or were weighing Data Center.
changes.read: Folding the top edition into Enterprise simplifies the lineup. Whether it’s a better deal for former Data Center buyers depends on Enterprise pricing at their size, which the page doesn’t show.

changes.headline: Moz tripled AI Visibility quotas on every Moz Pro plan at unchanged prices.
changes.who: Moz Pro customers tracking how AI assistants mention their brand.
changes.read: AI visibility tracking is a new, crowded category, and bigger quotas are a cheap way to win share while usage settles. Quotas, not prices, look like the competitive lever here for now.

changes.read: Probably a retired model rather than a pricing decision. It matters mainly as a sign of consumer security brands bundling AI into their subscriptions.

changes.who: New consumption-plan customers.
changes.read: A cut for new buyers only: a competitive acquisition move.

changes.headline: Syncfusion dropped its five-developer license minimum across all SDKs.
changes.who: Small teams and solo developers.
changes.read: Removing a minimum makes the entry price much lower for small buyers.

changes.headline: Plain replaced its seat bundles with straight per-user pricing.
changes.who: Support teams on Plain.
changes.read: Simpler to read; more expensive for small Foundation teams, cheaper for small Horizon ones.

changes.who: New Fundamentals buyers.
changes.read: A routine increase on a contract-priced product.

changes.stated: Atlassian points to its investment in AI, Teamwork Graph, integrated workflows and enterprise features.
changes.read: A standard annual increase justified by AI, but December matters more. Once AI gets a meter, seat prices pay for today's AI and the allowance protects margins as Rovo usage grows. The largest customers pay the steepest rise, the opposite of a volume discount, which suggests Atlassian sees little risk of big accounts leaving.

changes.read: A cash-flow and fraud fix, not a price rise. Paying upfront and stricter vetting close the gap where seats were used before they were paid for. changes.who: Every ChatGPT and Codex user. Developers on the API aren't affected.
changes.read: The model itself is now the packaging. Splitting the new generation by plan makes model quality, not just message limits, the reason to upgrade. Expect free and paid tiers to diverge further with each model release.

changes.who: Developers using heavy prompt caching, such as agents and coding tools that resend long context on every call.
changes.read: Two targeted cuts where competition is fiercest: the cheap, high-volume model tier and cache reads. Agent workloads reread the same context thousands of times, so both lower the real cost of building on Anthropic without cutting Sonnet’s headline prices.

changes.read: A routine annual increase. QuickBooks raised prices on 1 August, so the two main small-business accounting tools are moving together. That leaves customers with no cheaper place to switch to.

changes.read: Figma keeps adding products inside existing seats instead of selling them separately. That raises the value of a seat now. Our read: it often comes before a seat price increase once the beta ends.

changes.read: More included at the same price. Fifteen months covers a full annual audit cycle with room to spare, a common compliance request in security tools.

changes.read: Opening an add-on to cheaper plans widens who can pay for it without touching seat prices. It’s an expansion-revenue move aimed at mid-sized teams.

changes.read: The usual beta-to-meter path: free while people build the habit, then counted against credits. In the same week Specs was added to seats, so Figma is widening what a seat includes while metering the AI on top.

changes.headline: Max plans now include monthly API credits: $100 on Max 5x and $200 on Max 20x. Claude Dashboards and Motion (beta) were added to the plan feature lists.

changes.read: Folding API credits into a chat subscription links personal and developer spending in one account, which makes the subscription more valuable to people who build.

changes.read: Lower the entry barrier to win small teams, then recover the revenue through higher per-seat prices and AI upsells. A typical play for a mid-market CRM squeezed between HubSpot and Salesforce.

changes.read: Fewer plans and a higher entry price. Companies do this when the lowest tier attracts costly, low-value customers. Some small users will leave, and that's probably the point.

news.title: Notion’s Confusing Credit Model
news.gist: Notion has gone through four AI pricing setups: a paid add-on, AI folded into paid plans, Custom Agents sold on credits, and now two separate credit balances on every Business and Enterprise seat. One balance covers work where Notion picks the model; the other covers work where the user picks the model, plus Custom Agents. The two balances reset monthly, can’t be pooled and don’t roll over, and a third, shared workspace balance can top up either one. Litterst argues Notion should absorb this complexity instead of passing it to customers, for example with one pool or a separate balance only for Custom Agents.

news.title: Developer Tool Pricing Report, October 2026
news.gist: AgentDeals’ monthly tally of developer-tool pricing moves, updated through 27 Oct, counts far more changes than in September, and almost every change with a clear direction went against buyers. Most of the negative moves trim free allowances: smaller sign-up credits at Browser Use, tighter free rate limits at Groq, and no more monthly inference credits for free Hugging Face accounts. Paid bills rise without list-price changes too: Modal now meters egress, Fly.io raised its memory rate, and OVHcloud bills storage and IPv4 as separate lines. Meta also resumed charging for WhatsApp service messages beyond a free monthly allowance.

The two packaging changes that matter most are at Socket.dev, whose Free plan now covers a single developer seat instead of unlimited developers, and HiveMQ, which stopped new Serverless clusters and will retire that plan, free tier included, at year end. patterns.p: HubSpot no longer gives Starter its own email-send limit; sends now draw on the same Credits pool as other actions. Cust swapped cost ranges for a fixed credit cost per AI action and started charging credits for Teammates chats. Both changes come from PricingSaaS reports. More of what a plan includes is now stated in credits rather than in features or caps.

HubSpot cut free marketing email sends from 2,000 to 300 a month, while Zoom raised free Basic’s in-meeting AI questions from 3 to 20 and Dropzone AI removed the investigations cap on its base plan. Vendors loosen limits where they want people to try an AI feature and tighten them where the free plan was giving away the core product. HubSpot and Dropzone AI come from PricingSaaS reports; Zoom is our own capture.

patterns.t: Prices published at a finer grain
patterns.p: Avalara replaced a contact-sales bundle table with public prices per state, Intercom now bills WhatsApp per message instead of per conversation, and Day listed its new top plan at a price per agent. Each change ties the bill to a smaller, published unit, which is easier to compare but harder to forecast. Avalara and Day come from PricingSaaS reports; Intercom is our own capture.

news_trends.t: Credits spread, and get harder to read
news_trends.p: Notion now splits each seat’s AI usage into two credit balances, HubSpot moved Starter email sends onto shared Credits, and Cust gave each AI action a fixed credit price. Credits let vendors add new actions without new price lines, but buyers can’t easily translate them back into what they used to get.
